units.translation: where I emended to αἱματόφυρτον πᾶν ἔθνος τόδε [blood-defiled, all this nation], about which I said this in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition (1865) p. CI. "What is read in M, αἱματοσταγές [dripping with blood], has no place in the dactylic meter, from which it follows that Aeschylus used another compound of this kind. Whether it was αἱματόφυρτον [blood-defiled] or αἱμοφόρυκτον [blood-stained] or something else: whence, adding πᾶν [all], which is most common in such expressions, one should write, Ζεὺς γὰρ αἱματόφυρτον πᾶν ἔθνος τόδε λέσχας — [For Zeus, all this blood-defiled nation of the assembly —]. For what is added in the codex, αξιόμισον [worthy of hatred], is also owed to an interpreter, who had written ἀξιόμισον ήγήσατο [considered worthy of hatred] or something similar next to ἀπηξιώσατο [deemed unworthy]. Adjectives compounded with ἄξιος [worthy] are very common in later writers: in the surviving plays of the tragedians no such compounds are found except ἀξιόθρηνος [worthy of lamentation], ἀξιοπενθής [worthy of mourning], and αξιόχρεως [worthy, sufficient] in Euripides Alc. 907, Hipp. 1465, Orest. 596. Nor would Aeschylus, if he had wanted to use that adjective, have written ἀξιόμισον [worthy of hatred], but ἀξιομισές [worthy of hatred], just as he said παντομισῆ κνώδαλα [all-hated beasts], not παντόμισα [all-hated], Eumen. v. 644."
For Zeus, deeming this blood-dripping, hate-worthy nation unworthy of the assembly,
where Stanley reads ἀπ᾽ ἀξίων [from worthy parents], which the scholiast read, who explains it as ἀξίων οὖσαν γονέων [being from worthy parents].
to bewail and lament one's fortunes – has a worthy exercise.
suffering worthy things, having done worthy things (thus Hermann for ἀνάξια [unworthy]).
But I stood apart dishonored, in no way worthy.

it is worthy (Hermann reads άξια [worthy]: but since in the antistrophe there is an iambus, perhaps πρέπον [fitting] is better, of which ἄξιον [worthy] can be a gloss) to revere the power that holds the heavens.
revering you as worthy (thus Porson for ἀξίαν τ' [and worthy]: Wakefield reads ἀξίαν σ' [you worthy]) of worthy things,
and to be honored as most worthy of mortals now living.
where some copies have Ἀξιού [of Axius], others Ἀξειοῦ [of Axius], on which spelling see what is said in the Thesaurus vol. 1, 2 p. 1095.
to the ford of the Axius,
to deem worthy, to think fit
and in the middle form ἀξιόομαι I deem worthy, I think fit.
they did not deem it worthy even to look at the whole matter.
someone said that the gods do not deem it worthy to care for mortals.
with such words I deem it right to address him.
is this the account of the women? If anyone deems it worth learning.
these things have been deemed worthy by us in many ways.
I myself was not deemed worthy to obtain this.
so as to deem it right to join battle with the Persian army.
for he deemed it right to be the murderer of his mother.
I deem worthy, I think fit
driven or moved by the axle.
the pipes do not keep silence, driven by the axle.
but if you are without understanding and do not accept my word.
he brought about an unstoppable grief.
the naves of the heavy-laden axles creaked.
